### Part A - Arithmetic Operations

```{r}
# TODO: Store 17 in a variable called a, and 5 in a variable called b
# Then print the results of: a + b, a - b, a * b, a / b
a = 17
b = 5

a + b
a - b
a * b
a / b
```

```{r}
# TODO: Using the same a and b, compute and print a %% b and a %/% b
# a %% b = remainder of a / b
# a %/% b = whole-number (integer) division
a %% b
a %/% b
```

```{r}
# TODO: Print 2 raised to the power of 10 using the ^ operator
2 ^ 10
```

Question #1: Run 17 / 5, 17 %% 5, and 17 %/% 5 side by side. In your own words, explain how these three results relate to each other mathematically.

The three results relate to each other because they are used in division operations, where / returns a decimal quotient, %% returns the remainder of dividing the two numerics, and %/% returns the integer or whole number quotient.

Question #2: Predict the output of 10 %% 3 and 10 %/% 3 before running the code. Were you correct? If not, explain what you misunderstood.

I predicted that the output of 10 %% 3 is 1 since modulo operator returns the remainder when two numerics are divided and that the output of 10 %/% 3 is 3 because it returns the integer or whole number quotient from dividing the two numerics.


### Part B - Basic Data Types: typeof(), class(), and mode()

```{r}
x <- 42
y <- 42L        # the L suffix forces an integer
z <- "42"
w <- TRUE
v <- 3 + 2i     # complex number

# TODO: Use typeof() to check the type of each of x, y, z, w, v
typeof(x)
typeof(y)
typeof(z)
typeof(w)
typeof(v)
```

```{r}
# TODO: Use class() to check the class of each of x, y, z, w, v
class(x)
class(y)
class(z)
class(w)
class(v)
```

```{r}
# TODO: Use mode() to check the class of each of x, y, z, w, v
mode(x)
mode(y)
mode(z)
mode(w)
mode(v)
```

Question #3: x <- 42 and y <- 42L look almost identical, but typeof(x) and typeof(y) give different answers. Explain the difference in your own words.

The two look almost identical but assigning 42 to x and then running typeof() to check its datatype only means that the value assigned is a double as default, and adding L to it like 42L which is assigned to y specifies that its datatype is an integer.

Question #4: Is typeof() ever different from class() and from mode() for the same object? Look at your results above and explain any case where this happens (or, if you did not see one, explain what you would expect for a matrix or factor).

Yes, typeof() differs since its result is "double", while the result of class() and mode() is "numeric". The function typeof() checks the actual type of object, class() checks the kind or type of object, and mode() checks the general type of object.


### Part C - Type Conversion (20 min)

```{r}
num_string <- "123"
# TODO: Convert num_string to a numeric value using as.numeric()
# Then check its type with typeof(), class(), and mode()

num_value <- as.numeric(num_string)

typeof(num_value)
class(num_value)
mode(num_value)
```

```{r}
# TODO: Convert the number 0 and the number 1 to logical using as.logical()
# What do you get?
as.logical(0)
as.logical(1)
```
I got [1] FALSE for as.logical(0) and [1] TRUE for as.logical(1)

```{r}
bad_string <- "hello123"
# TODO: Try converting bad_string to numeric using as.numeric()
# Run this chunk and observe the warning message and the result

as.numeric(bad_string)
```
Running the code chunk displays a warning message "Warning: NAs introduced by coercion" and a result: [1] NA

Question #5: When you ran the conversion-fail chunk, R produced NA and a warning instead of stopping with an error.

Why do you think R is designed to give a warning here rather than crashing the whole script?

I think it is because R is made to work with large amounts of data, so it still processes the valid values to avoid losing data, while giving a warning for the bad values so they can be fixed later on.

What are the risks of this behavior if you don’t read your warnings?

If warnings are not read, the risks are not knowing that some data failed to convert and they become unusable and there will be missing or incorrect results if the bad values are used in other important parts of the script.


### Part D - Strings, paste(), and paste0()

```{r}
first_name <- "Juan"
last_name <- "Dela Cruz"

# TODO: Print first_name and last_name using print() and/or cat()
print(first_name)
print(last_name)
```

```{r}
# TODO: Use paste() to combine first_name and last_name into a full name
# TODO: Use paste0() to do the same, and compare the two results

full_name <- paste(first_name, last_name)
full_name0 <- paste0(first_name, last_name)

print(full_name)
print(full_name0)
```
Running paste results in [1] Juan Dela Cruz (with a space that separates the first name and last name), while running paste0 results in [1] JuanDela Cruz (no space between the first and last name).

```{r}
# TODO: Use paste() with the argument sep = "-" to join first_name and
# last_name with a dash instead of a space

paste(first_name, last_name, sep = "-")
```

```{r}
age <- 21
# TODO: Use paste0() to build the sentence:
# "Juan Dela Cruz is 21 years old." by combining full_name, age, and text

sentence0 <- paste0(full_name, " is ", age, " years old.")
print(sentence0)
```

Question #7: paste() and paste0() produced different results for the same two strings. Explain exactly why, referencing what each function does by default.

The functions paste() and paste0() are different in a way that paste() joins values but puts a space between them by default, while paste0() joins values without separating or putting space between them by default.

Question #8: In the strings-numbers chunk, you combined a character string with a numeric variable (age) using paste0() without first converting age to a string.

Did this cause an error? Explain what paste0() does internally to make this work, and how it relates to the type conversions you practiced in Part C.

No, it did not cause an error. The function paste0() automatically converts any argument into a string regardless of its original data type so it can be combined. It relates to the type conversions I practiced in Part C because values can be converted from one data type to another and in this case, paste0() converts the numeric value of age into a character string without using as.character().


### Part E - Critical Thinking Challenge

```{r}
# TODO: Predict, then test: what is the result of "5" + 5 in R?
# Run it and read the error message carefully.

# "5" +  5
```

Running the code chunk displays an error message "Error in "5" + 5: non-numeric argument to binary operator"

```{r}
# TODO: Now fix the code above so that "5" + 5 correctly evaluates to 10
# using an appropriate conversion function.

as.numeric("5") + 5
```

Question #9: Some programming languages automatically convert "5" + 5 into 10 without an error. R does not.

Based on what you’ve learned about R’s data types in this lab, why do you think R requires an explicit conversion instead of guessing what the programmer meant?

I think R requires explicit conversion instead of guessing because when working with large amounts of data, a small mistake can lead to a different result, so manually converting the data type helps avoid these errors.

Question #10: Suppose a classmate writes a script that reads a column of “numbers” from a text file. The column looks numeric, but when they try sum() on it, R throws an error. Based on everything in this lab (types, typeof()/class()/mode(), conversion, warnings), write a short paragraph explaining what likely went wrong and the steps you’d take to diagnose and fix it.

The reason why R gives an error is most likely because the data type does not match the sum() function. The values may be numbers inside "", making them character strings instead of numeric. First, read the error message, then use typeof(), class(), and mode() to check the data type of the "numbers." If they are character strings, they must be converted into numeric using as.numeric() and running the code again to check if it works.

# Conclusion
In 3-4 sentences, summarize what you have learned about how R handles different data types, and why understanding typeof()/class() and conversion functions matter before doing arithmetic or combining data.

I learned that R handles different data types depending on the operation being performed. The typeof() and class() functions help to identify data types, while conversion functions allow data to be changed from one type to another. It is important to understand them to avoid errors and make sure that results are accurate when doing arithmetic or combining data.
